questions: What happens if Takahashi attempts to move outside the grid boundaries during a change operation?
Is the initial position (sh, sw) of Takahashi considered part of the path calculation, or does he only affect cells he moves into?
Are there any constraints on the starting position (sh, sw) relative to the grid dimensions beyond the basic bounds?
How should the program handle the case when H or W equals 1, making the path definition potentially degenerate?
Does the path always have to go from (1,1) to (H,W), regardless of Takahashi's current position?
What is the exact order of operations within each change: does Takahashi move first, then update the cell, then compute the path sum?
Are self-intersecting paths allowed, or must each path consist of exactly H+W-1 distinct cells?
Should the output include the path sum calculation before any changes are made, or only after each of the Q changes?
answers: The move is always guaranteed to be valid. In each change, the direction d_i ensures that the destination cell exists within the grid boundaries.
The initial position is independent of paths; paths always go from (1,1) to (H,W).
Only the basic bounds apply: 1 ≤ sh ≤ H and 1 ≤ sw ≤ W.
The path formula applies: C(H+W-2, H-1) valid paths exist even for degenerate grids.
Yes. There are exactly C(H+W-2, H-1) valid paths between (1,1) and (H,W) under the defined movement rules.
Takahashi moves to a new position, updates that cell's value, then the path sum is computed with the updated grid.
Paths only move right or down, so they cannot revisit cells and always have exactly H+W-1 cells.
Output the path sum after each of the Q changes.
inline_prompts:
There is an H \times W grid. Let (h,w) denote the cell at the h-th row from the top and the w-th column from the left. A non-negative integer A_{h,w} is written in cell (h,w). Takahashi starts at cell (sh,sw) and will perform Q changes to the grid. The i-th change is given by a character d_i (d_i is one of L, R, U, D) and a non-negative integer a_i, meaning Takahashi will do the following:
- Move one cell in the direction d_i. That is, if d_i is L, move left; if R, move right; if U, move up; if D, move down by one cell. Then, let the destination cell be (h,w), and set A_{h,w} to a_i. The move is always guaranteed to be valid. In each change, the direction d_i ensures that the destination cell exists within the grid boundaries.
After each change, print the answer to the following problem:
A sequence of cells P = ((h_1,w_1), \ldots, (h_{M},w_{M})) is said to be a path if and only if it satisfies all of the following conditions:
- (h_1,w_1) = (1,1), (h_{M},w_{M}) = (H,W), and M = H + W - 1.
- For every i with 1 \leq i \leq M-1, either (h_{i+1}, w_{i+1}) = (h_i + 1, w_i) or (h_{i+1}, w_{i+1}) = (h_i, w_i + 1).
For a path P = ((h_1,w_1), \ldots, (h_{M},w_{M})), define f(P) = \prod_{1\leq i\leq M}A_{h_i,w_i}. Print the sum, modulo 998244353, of f(P) over all paths P.
Input
The input is given from Standard Input in the following format:
H W
A_{1,1} \cdots A_{1,W}
\vdots
A_{H,1} \cdots A_{H,W}
Q sh sw
d_1 a_1
\vdots
d_Q a_Q
Output
Print Q lines.
The i-th line should contain the sum, modulo 998244353, of f(P) over all paths P after performing the i-th change to the grid.
Constraints
- 2 \leq H, W \leq 200000
- HW \leq 200000
- 0 \
